title: A triangle of satellite flares near Gemini North
caption: Satellite flares and the Milky Way beside Gemini North, Maunakea, Hawai‘i
celestial: Photograph taken at Gemini North, Maunakea, Hawai‘i

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Three bright flares of light form a triangle to the right of Gemini North in this view from near the summit of Maunakea in Hawai‘i, with the Milky Way behind. The flares are sunlight glinting off satellites.

Observatories like Gemini North are built in remote places to escape light pollution, the glow of city and suburban lights. Here the telescope sits above layers of cloud that block the lights of the towns below. But satellite constellations are a different kind of artificial light, and remoteness can’t hide a telescope from them.

This long-exposure photograph seems to show a clear sky, yet telescopes are typically about a billion times more sensitive than the human eye. Satellites that people never notice show up to them as bright streaks or a general brightening of the sky.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/J. Pollard. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would to someone standing on site.

explore: Gemini North is one half of the International Gemini Observatory, operated by NOIRLab. NOIRLab works with satellite operators and other observatories on ways to protect dark skies.
alt: A large telescope dome at night with the Milky Way behind it and three bright points of light forming a triangle to its right.
